body.heading: Every tradition was invented once
paragraphs: It is easy to assume traditions must be old to count. In fact every one of them began as somebody's new idea that happened twice. A tradition is just a good moment that a family decided to repeat — the pancakes on Saturdays, the walk on the first day of spring, the terrible joke that must be told when the car passes a certain sign.
That means your family does not need permission or ancestry to start one. It needs a moment worth repeating and the small discipline of repeating it.

body.heading: How to choose a candidate
paragraphs: Look for things that already happened happily more than once: the meal everyone requests, the game that ends every visit, the route you always walk with a particular person. Naming what is already nearly a tradition is easier than inventing one from nothing.

Attach it to a peg that returns by itself — a day, a season, a journey, the first of something — rather than relying on memory. And keep it small enough to survive a busy year: a tradition that can shrink is a tradition that lasts.

body.heading: Let it belong to everyone
paragraphs: Invite the whole family to adjust it. Children who help shape a ritual defend it fiercely and carry it further. Note the first occurrence somewhere — a line in a notebook, a dated photograph — because in twenty years, 'when did we start doing this?' is a question somebody will be delighted to answer.
And do not worry if it mutates over the years. Traditions that bend survive; the pancake that becomes a waffle is still, in every way that matters, the same tradition.
